Well, hello, Doctor. I, uh... I suppose I'm here because my manager told me I needed to get things sorted out. I've been working as a cashier—which, you know, I have a bachelor's degree, so it's not exactly where I thought I'd be at 54, but it pays the bills. Anyway, the problem is... I keep getting stuck at the register. Just completely stuck doing things that don't fit the moment at all. 

It's hard to explain, but, like, I'll be ringing someone up, and instead of just scanning the item, I'll start tapping it against the scanner. Not just once, but in this whole specific pattern, tap-tap-tap, over and over, and I can't just ring it normally. Or, worse, I'll hit the total button, the cash drawer pops open, and my hand goes in to get the change, and I just... freeze. I'll just be standing there with my hand hovering right over the cash drawer, completely frozen like a statue. And the customer is just standing there waiting, you know, looking at me, clearing their throat, holding their bags, and I know they want their change so they can leave, but I just can't unfreeze my hand. 

It's really embarrassing, honestly, all these people staring at me while I'm stuck like that. And it caused a huge line the other day, people were complaining, so last week my manager actually wrote me up for it. Put a formal warning in my file and everything. So, I need to figure out why my body keeps doing these things when I'm supposed to be working, because I really can't afford to lose this job.
When you get the urge to do the tapping or freeze in place, does it feel like something you have to do to prevent something bad from happening?

No, no, it's not like that. It's not a superstitious thing, you know, like, "Oh, if I don't tap this can of soup three times, the roof is going to cave in," or anything like that. I don't have those kinds of thoughts. I know some people do, like they have to check the stove a hundred times or the house will burn down, but for me, it's... it's just my body doing it. 

It's almost like... like my brain sends a signal, but the signal gets caught in a loop, or it just stops halfway down my arm. I don't feel anxious before it happens, not like I'm trying to stop a disaster. I just... do it. Like the tapping. I'll pick up the item, and my hand just starts doing the pattern. Tap-tap-tap. And I'm watching my hand do it, and I'm thinking, "Okay, that's enough, just scan the barcode so this nice lady can buy her cat food," but my hand just keeps tapping. 

And the freezing, the freezing is even weirder, because there's no urge at all. It's the complete absence of an urge. My hand goes into the drawer for the quarters, and then it's just... off. Like someone unplugged my arm from the socket. I'm not thinking about anything bad happening, I'm just thinking, "Move, hand, move," and it just doesn't. It's incredibly frustrating, really, because my mind is perfectly clear, I know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing, but the machinery just completely breaks down on me.
Before the tapping or freezing happens, do you feel a build-up of physical tension or an urge that gets relieved when you do it?

No, no, it's really not like that at all. You know how when you have to sneeze, there's that tickle, that... that pressure that builds up right in the bridge of your nose, and you just know it's coming, and then when you finally sneeze, it's this huge relief? It's nothing like that. There's no build-up. There's no tight feeling in my muscles or, you know, some kind of itch in my bones that I have to scratch by tapping the scanner. 

I wish there was a warning like that, honestly, because then maybe I could excuse myself, tell the customer I need a second, go to the breakroom, let it out, and come back. But it's just... sudden. Like, I'll be holding a box of cereal—say, Cheerios, the big family size one, they always buy the big ones—and my arm is moving perfectly fine, totally relaxed, just doing the physical motion I've done a thousand times, and then suddenly the tapping just starts. There's no relief when it happens, either. I don't feel better for having done it. 

And with the freezing... well, the freezing is the exact opposite of relief. My arm doesn't get stiff beforehand, it doesn't ache, there's absolutely no tension at all before it happens. The power just cuts out. It's not a release of anything. If anything, the freezing creates tension, because I'm standing there, totally locked up, and I'm stressing out because the customer is staring at me, and my shoulder actually starts to hurt from holding my arm out in mid-air over the quarter slot for so long without moving. But before it happens? No. Nothing. No tension, no urge. It's just like a switch flips without anyone even touching it.
When did these tapping or freezing episodes first start?

Well, let me think about that. Time sort of blends together when you're doing shift work, you know? You punch in, you punch out, you stand under those awful fluorescent lights, and it's just a sea of barcodes and receipts and plastic bags. But if I really sit down and trace it back... I'd say it's been about three months. Yeah, roughly three months. 

I know this because it was right around the time my manager, Gary—he's the one who wrote me up, actually, nice enough guy usually but very strictly by-the-book, always worried about corporate coming down on him—anyway, he had just switched my schedule from the early morning shift to the mid-day rush.
